claim: Human adults exhibited biases in their perception of local transitions between elements in auditory sequences.
source: We show that human adults exhibited biases in their perception of local transitions between elements, which made them sensitive to high-order network structures such as communities.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental results presented in the manuscript, supported by behavioral data from the forced-choice task and key press distributions.

claim: Human adults are sensitive to high-order network structures such as communities in auditory sequences.
source: We show that human adults exhibited biases in their perception of local transitions between elements, which made them sensitive to high-order network structures such as communities.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data showing differential responses to within-community versus between-community transitions.

claim: Human behavior in auditory sequence learning is consistent with the creation of a parsimonious simplified model from the evidence they receive.
source: This behavior is consistent with the creation of a parsimonious simpliﬁed model from the evidence they receive, achieved by pruning and completing relationships between network elements.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data showing pruning of familiar between-community transitions and completion of new within-community transitions.

claim: The brain does not rely on exact memories but on a parsimonious representation of the world.
source: This observation suggests that the brain does not rely on exact memories but on a parsimonious representation of the world.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data showing biased perception of transitions and is a theoretical interpretation of the findings.

claim: The bias in human perception of auditory sequences can be analytically modeled by a memory/efficiency trade-off.
source: Moreover, this bias can be analytically modeled by a memory/efficiency trade-off.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis showing that the FEMM (free energy minimization model) best fits the behavioral data.

claim: The memory/efficiency trade-off model correctly accounts for previous findings, including local transition probabilities as well as high-order network structures.
source: This model correctly accounts for previous findings, including local transition probabilities as well as high-order network structures, unifying sequence learning across scales.
evidence: This is supported by the model comparison analysis and references to previous literature on statistical learning.

claim: The sensitivity of humans to local dependencies has been robustly demonstrated in the auditory and visual domain.
source: Since then, the sensitivity of humans to local dependencies has been robustly demonstrated in the auditory and visual domain (Fiser and Aslin, 2002) without the focus of attention (Batterink and Choi, 2021; Batterink and Paller, 2019; Benjamin et al., 2021) and even in asleep neonates (Benjamin et al., 2023; Fló et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Sensitivity to local dependencies occurs without the focus of attention.
source: Since then, the sensitivity of humans to local dependencies has been robustly demonstrated in the auditory and visual domain (Fiser and Aslin, 2002) without the focus of attention (Batterink and Choi, 2021; Batterink and Paller, 2019; Benjamin et al., 2021) and even in asleep neonates (Benjamin et al., 2023; Fló et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Batterink and Choi, 2021; Batterink and Paller, 2019; Benjamin et al., 2021.

claim: Sensitivity to local dependencies occurs even in asleep neonates.
source: Since then, the sensitivity of humans to local dependencies has been robustly demonstrated in the auditory and visual domain (Fiser and Aslin, 2002) without the focus of attention (Batterink and Choi, 2021; Batterink and Paller, 2019; Benjamin et al., 2021) and even in asleep neonates (Benjamin et al., 2023; Fló et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Benjamin et al., 2023; Fló et al., 2022.

claim: Network science proposed a different description to characterize complex streams.
source: Network science - an emerging interdisciplinary field - thus proposed a different description to characterize more complex streams (Lynn et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lynn et al., 2020.

claim: In the network framework, a stream of stimuli corresponds to a random walk in the associated probabilistic network.
source: In this framework, a stream of stimuli corresponds to a random walk in the associated probabilistic network.
evidence: This is a description of the network science framework, drawing from established knowledge in the field.

claim: Schapiro et al., 2013, tested human adults with a network consisting of three communities where transitions between all elements were equiprobable.
source: Schapiro et al., 2013, tested human adults with a network consisting of three communities (i.e. sets of nodes densely connected with each other and poorly connected with the rest of the graph; Newman, 2003) where transitions between all elements were equiprobable (each node had the same degree).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schapiro et al., 2013.

claim: Subjects discriminated transitions between communities from those within communities in Schapiro et al., 2013.
source: The authors reported that subjects discriminated transitions between communities from those within communities.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schapiro et al., 2013.

claim: The result from Schapiro et al., 2013 revealed participants' sensitivity to higher-order properties not covered by local probabilistic models.
source: Since local properties (TP) were not informative, this result revealed participants' sensitivity to higher-order properties not covered by local probabilistic models.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results from Schapiro et al., 2013, based on inference from the experimental design.

claim: Sensitivity to community structure seems already to be in place at 6 years old.
source: This sensitivity seems already to be in place at 6y-o (Pudhiyidath et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pudhiyidath et al., 2020.

claim: Lynn et al., 2020, replicated a similar effect with a probabilistic sequential response task.
source: Recently, Lynn et al., 2020, replicated a similar effect with a probabilistic sequential response task.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lynn et al., 2020.

claim: Lynn et al., 2020 proposed an analytical model that optimizes the trade-off between accuracy and computational complexity by minimizing the free energy function.
source: To explain the response pattern, the authors proposed an analytical model that optimizes the trade-off between accuracy and computational complexity by minimizing the free energy function.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lynn et al., 2020.

claim: Adults do not encode the exact input but a parsimonious version based on the generalization of the underlying structure.
source: Moreover, we propose that adults do not encode the exact input but a parsimonious version based on the generalization of the underlying structure.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors, to be tested by the experimental data.

claim: Network learning has been studied in the visual domain.
source: Moreover, while several papers have studied network learning in the visual domain (Karuza et al., 2019; Lynn et al., 2020; Schapiro et al., 2013), to our knowledge, it has never been tested in the auditory domain despite the better statistical learning capacities in the auditory modality (Conway and Christiansen, 2005), the sophisticated auditory sequence processing abilities observed in humans compared to other primates (Dehaene et al., 2015), and their potential importance in language acquisition.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Karuza et al., 2019; Lynn et al., 2020; Schapiro et al., 2013.

claim: Network learning has never been tested in the auditory domain prior to this study.
source: Moreover, while several papers have studied network learning in the visual domain (Karuza et al., 2019; Lynn et al., 2020; Schapiro et al., 2013), to our knowledge, it has never been tested in the auditory domain despite the better statistical learning capacities in the auditory modality (Conway and Christiansen, 2005), the sophisticated auditory sequence processing abilities observed in humans compared to other primates (Dehaene et al., 2015), and their potential importance in language acquisition.
evidence: This is a claim about the state of the literature, based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: Humans have better statistical learning capacities in the auditory modality compared to visual.
source: Moreover, while several papers have studied network learning in the visual domain (Karuza et al., 2019; Lynn et al., 2020; Schapiro et al., 2013), to our knowledge, it has never been tested in the auditory domain despite the better statistical learning capacities in the auditory modality (Conway and Christiansen, 2005), the sophisticated auditory sequence processing abilities observed in humans compared to other primates (Dehaene et al., 2015), and their potential importance in language acquisition.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Conway and Christiansen, 2005.

claim: Humans have sophisticated auditory sequence processing abilities compared to other primates.
source: Moreover, while several papers have studied network learning in the visual domain (Karuza et al., 2019; Lynn et al., 2020; Schapiro et al., 2013), to our knowledge, it has never been tested in the auditory domain despite the better statistical learning capacities in the auditory modality (Conway and Christiansen, 2005), the sophisticated auditory sequence processing abilities observed in humans compared to other primates (Dehaene et al., 2015), and their potential importance in language acquisition.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dehaene et al., 2015.

claim: The study used a 4 Hz presentation rate to force rapid processing of each element of the sequence.
source: Here, we used a 4 Hz presentation, typically used in auditory sequence learning tasks, in order to force rapid processing of each element of the sequence and to be more comparable to the sequence learning literature.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design used in the study.

claim: Approximately 240 adult participants were tested in each paradigm.
source: For this purpose, we tested three different experimental paradigms in an online task, using sequences of pure tones or of syllables (~240 adult participants tested in each paradigm).
evidence: This is a description of the sample size in the study.

claim: The full community paradigm tested a network composed of two communities of six elements each, with all nodes within a community connected with each other except two nodes at the border.
source: The first paradigm - full community - tested a network composed of two communities of six elements each, with all nodes within a community connected with each other (except two nodes at the border of the community to keep an equal degree for each node).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In the sparse community paradigm, one possible edge for each node was removed.
source: In the second and third paradigms, the communities were incomplete, some connections being never presented during the exposure to the continuous sequence: In the sparse and high sparse community paradigms, respectively one and two possible edges for each node were removed.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In the high sparse community paradigm, two possible edges for each node were removed.
source: In the second and third paradigms, the communities were incomplete, some connections being never presented during the exposure to the continuous sequence: In the sparse and high sparse community paradigms, respectively one and two possible edges for each node were removed.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Participants were first asked to carefully listen to a continuous sequence for about 4 minutes.
source: In each paradigm, participants were first asked to carefully listen to a continuous sequence for about 4 mn and then to press a key when they felt there was a natural break in the sequence (~2 mn).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Participants were asked to press a key when they felt there was a natural break in the sequence.
source: In each paradigm, participants were first asked to carefully listen to a continuous sequence for about 4 mn and then to press a key when they felt there was a natural break in the sequence (~2 mn).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The key press task allowed measuring participants' ability to parse the sequence.
source: This task allowed measuring participants' ability to parse the sequence and to compare their performances in the auditory domain with those published in the visual domain.
evidence: This is a description of the purpose of the key press task.

claim: In the test phase, participants were asked to choose between two isolated quadruplets, the most congruent with what they had heard before.
source: In a following test phase, they were asked to choose between two isolated quadruplets, the most congruent with what they had heard before, during the familiarization sequence.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The test phase allowed presenting previously unheard transitions ('new transitions').
source: With this test phase, we could present previously unheard transitions ('new transitions') and study whether participants were able to generalize the network structure (Figure 1), notably in the two incomplete networks (sparse and high sparse paradigms).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and its purpose.

claim: The two tasks (key press and forced-choice) were done twice.
source: These two tasks were done twice.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: In the forced-choice task, each other condition was tested against the familiar within community transitions.
source: In the forced-choice task between the isolated quadruplets, we tested each other conditions against the familiar within community transitions (condition considered as the reference; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: If participants did not learn the graph structure, they should be random in their familiarity choice between familiar within and between community transitions.
source: If participants did not learn the graph structure of the sequence, they had to be random in their familiarity choice between familiar within and between community transitions because all quadruplets have been presented and had the same local TPs between their elements.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the experimental design and theoretical considerations.

claim: If participants learned the graph, their familiarity score should be below 50% for between community transitions.
source: By contrast, if they had indeed learned the graph, their familiarity score should be below 50% denoting their preference for the familiar within community transitions (i.e. reference).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the experimental design and theoretical considerations.

claim: Participants significantly rejected the new between community transitions in each paradigm.
source: As can be seen in Figure 3, participants signiﬁcantly rejected the new between community transitions in each paradigm (ps <0.01 FDR), this transition is both novel and jumping across communities.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The familiar between community transition condition was only significantly rejected in the sparse community paradigm.
source: The familiar between community transition condition was only signiﬁcantly rejected in the sparse community paradigm (p<0.01 FDR).
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The new within community transitions were chosen/rejected at chance in the sparse and high sparse community paradigms.
source: Second, the new within community transitions were chosen/rejected at chance in the sparse and high sparse community paradigms indicating a similar perception of familiarity for these never heard transitions and the reference.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data presented in Figure 3.

claim: In the sparse community paradigm, the familiarity score was larger for the new within community transitions than for both between community transitions.
source: Third, in the sparse community paradigm, the familiarity score was larger for the new within community transitions than for both between community transitions (new: p<0.01 FDR; and familiar: p<0.05 FDR).
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The comparisons between new within and between community transitions were only marginally significant in the high sparse paradigm.
source: These comparisons were only marginally significant in the high sparse paradigm (uncorrected p=0.046).
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Participants encoded the graph structure as revealed by the difference in familiarity between within and between community transitions.
source: In other words, the participants encoded the graph structure as revealed by the difference in familiarity between within and between community transitions and naturally completed the graph as indicated by the scores at chance for never heard transitions compatible with the graph structure.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data.

claim: Participants naturally completed the graph as indicated by the scores at chance for never heard transitions compatible with the graph structure.
source: In other words, the participants encoded the graph structure as revealed by the difference in familiarity between within and between community transitions and naturally completed the graph as indicated by the scores at chance for never heard transitions compatible with the graph structure.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data.

claim: All models were significantly correlated with the data.
source: All models were signiﬁcantly correlated with the data (all p<0.01 FDRcorr), with a correlation strength following the order FEMM ≈ hitting time > communicability > non-adjacent TPs ≈ TPs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: The correlation strength between models and data followed the order FEMM ≈ hitting time > communicability > non-adjacent TPs ≈ TPs.
source: All models were signiﬁcantly correlated with the data (all p<0.01 FDRcorr), with a correlation strength following the order FEMM ≈ hitting time > communicability > non-adjacent TPs ≈ TPs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: FEMM and hitting time had the best correlation with the data (81%).
source: They had the best correlation with the data (81%) and were signiﬁcantly better than all the other theoretical models (p<0.05 FDR).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: FEMM and hitting time were significantly better than all the other theoretical models.
source: They had the best correlation with the data (81%) and were signiﬁcantly better than all the other theoretical models (p<0.05 FDR).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: Both Hebbian and hippocampus neural models were significantly highly correlated with the data.
source: Both models were signiﬁcantly highly correlated with the data and with each other.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: The Hebbian implementation of FEMM was slightly but significantly more correlated to the data than the hippocampus model.
source: However, the Hebbian implementation of FEMM was slightly but significantly more correlated to our data than the hippocampus model (Figure 4) typically because of the lack of agreement between the hippocampus model and the data in the high sparse paradigm.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: The average bootstrap correlation between the data and the FEMM is 77%.
source: Our best fit with any model is the 77% average bootstrap correlation between our data and the FEMM, which is relatively close to the ceiling fit given this dataset, showing a very high relevance of the FEMM to account for the data.
evidence: This claim is supported by the bootstrap correlation analysis.

claim: The noise ceiling for the model fit is 84% correlation.
source: We find an average of 84% correlations as a noise ceiling for those data.
evidence: This claim is supported by the bootstrap analysis estimating the noise ceiling.

claim: Human adults do not encode transition probabilities objectively when familiarized with a stream of sounds.
source: Our results show that human adults do not encode TPs objectively when familiarized with a stream of sounds.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the behavioral data.

claim: Adults have a systematic bias to complete the transitions within a community.
source: Instead, they seem to have a systematic bias to complete the transitions within a community suggesting a subjective internal representation that differs from the objective distribution of the transitions they heard.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the behavioral data.

claim: The bias in the encoding of transition probabilities between successive elements enabled the extraction and encoding of high-order structures in graphs.
source: The bias in the encoding of TP between successive elements enabled the extraction and encoding of high-order structures in graphs, that is, a community structure.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: There are two distinct bias effects: pruning of familiar transitions that do not conform to the community structure and completion of the structure by overgeneralizing new transitions when they are compatible with the high-order structure.
source: We can distinguish two distinct bias effects: First, the pruning of familiar transitions that do not conform to the community structure (i.e. familiar between community transitions are rejected). Second, the completion of the structure by overgeneralizing new transitions when they are compatible with the high-order structure (i.e. new within community transitions are accepted).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: These perceptual biases lead to a more parsimonious internal representation of graphs.
source: These perceptual biases lead to a more parsimonious internal representation of graphs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The computation of transition probabilities is biased in humans.
source: We showed that the computation of TPs is biased in humans, and analytically, this bias is characterized as an optimal trade-off between accuracy and computational complexity.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: The bias is characterized as an optimal trade-off between accuracy and computational complexity.
source: We showed that the computation of TPs is biased in humans, and analytically, this bias is characterized as an optimal trade-off between accuracy and computational complexity.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the FEMM model.

claim: Perfect accuracy in the encoding would result in no sensitivity to the high-order structure.
source: Indeed, perfect accuracy in the encoding would result in no sensitivity to the high-order structure, while too low accuracy would result in no learning at all.
evidence: This is a theoretical argument about the trade-off in the FEMM model.

claim: Too low accuracy would result in no learning at all.
source: Indeed, perfect accuracy in the encoding would result in no sensitivity to the high-order structure, while too low accuracy would result in no learning at all.
evidence: This is a theoretical argument about the trade-off in the FEMM model.

claim: Hebbian learning is a very simple mechanism that consists of reinforcing co-occurrences in a signal.
source: Hebbian learning is a very simple mechanism that consists of reinforcing co-occurrences in a signal.
evidence: This is a description of Hebbian learning based on established knowledge.

claim: Hebbian learning has been proposed as a learning mechanism in statistical learning tasks.
source: It has been proposed as a learning mechanism in statistical learning tasks (Endress and Johnson, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Endress and Johnson, 2021.

claim: Hebbian learning could be implemented in many brain regions through learning-induced synaptic plasticity.
source: Such learning could be implemented in many brain regions through learning-induced synaptic plasticity and does not require any specific structural organization of neurons.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on knowledge of neural mechanisms.

claim: The CA1 similarity model relies on the specific architecture of the hippocampus.
source: In contrast, the CA1 similarity model relies on the specific architecture of the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a description of the CA1 similarity model.

claim: Several authors have proposed that statistical learning and graph learning might be represented as the construction of an abstract map of relational knowledge, analogous to topographic maps.
source: Testing a hippocampus specific model is essential because several authors have proposed that statistical learning and graph learning might be represented as the construction of an abstract map of relational knowledge, analogous to topographic maps (Constantinescu et al., 2016; Garvert et al., 2017), which are known to involve the hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Constantinescu et al., 2016; Garvert et al., 2017.

claim: Topographic maps are known to involve the hippocampus.
source: Testing a hippocampus specific model is essential because several authors have proposed that statistical learning and graph learning might be represented as the construction of an abstract map of relational knowledge, analogous to topographic maps (Constantinescu et al., 2016; Garvert et al., 2017), which are known to involve the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a claim based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: The hippocampus has been proposed as a good candidate for the implementation of the successor representation.
source: Moreover, the hippocampus has also been proposed as a good candidate for the implementation of the successor representation, giving this structure the role of a predictive map unifying temporal and spatial relational knowledge under a common framework (Stachenfeld et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stachenfeld et al., 2017.

claim: When exposed to statistically organized auditory or visual streams, the hippocampus activity measured with ECoG exhibited a cluster-like behavior.
source: A recent experimental study (Henin et al., 2021) showed that when exposed to statistically organized auditory or visual streams, the hippocampus activity measured with ECoG exhibited a cluster-like behavior, with all elements belonging to the same group being similarly encoded.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Henin et al., 2021.

claim: Schapiro et al., 2016, reported an increased pattern similarity in the hippocampus for elements belonging to the same community using the community paradigm with fMRI.
source: Using the community paradigm with fMRI, Schapiro et al., 2016, also reported an increased pattern similarity in the hippocampus for elements belonging to the same community (see also Pudhiyidath et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schapiro et al., 2016.

claim: Schapiro et al., 2017, used a neural model mimicking the hippocampus architecture and trained it on different statistical learning tasks including community structure learning.
source: Another piece of evidence comes from modeling the hippocampus activity in different statistical learning tasks (Schapiro et al., 2017). In this study, the authors used a neural model mimicking the hippocampus architecture and trained it on different statistical learning tasks including community structure learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schapiro et al., 2017.

claim: The pattern of activity in CA1 might account for both pair learning (episodic memory) and community structure learning.
source: They showed that the pattern of activity in CA1 might account for both pair learning (episodic memory) and community structure learning, and thus is partially consistent with two mechanisms observed in the hippocampus: pattern completion (i.e. the similarity of the neural representations of close stimuli increases, which allows generalization) and pattern separation (i.e. the similarity of neural representation of close stimuli decreases, to disambiguate them) (Bakker et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2016; Yassa and Stark, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schapiro et al., 2017 and references to pattern completion and separation.

claim: Both a general Hebbian model and a more specific hippocampal model fit very well the pattern of familiarity scores given by the participants.
source: Here, we showed that both a general Hebbian model and a more specific hippocampal model ﬁt very well the pattern of familiarity scores given by the participants with a slightly better result, yet significant, for the Hebbian learning approach.
evidence: This is a summary of the model comparison results.

claim: The Hebbian learning approach had a slightly better, yet significant, result compared to the hippocampal model.
source: Here, we showed that both a general Hebbian model and a more specific hippocampal model ﬁt very well the pattern of familiarity scores given by the participants with a slightly better result, yet significant, for the Hebbian learning approach.
evidence: This is a summary of the model comparison results.

claim: Recent work proposed the joint use of several computation involving cortical and hippocampal learning in similar tasks.
source: In any case, the agreement between the behavioral data and two brain models shows that the FEMM (an analytical model) does not only explain behavioral data but also has biologically valid candidates.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Varga et al., 2022; Whittington et al., 2020.

claim: The FEMM does not only explain behavioral data but also has biologically valid candidates.
source: In any case, the agreement between the behavioral data and two brain models shows that the FEMM (an analytical model) does not only explain behavioral data but also has biologically valid candidates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model comparison results.

claim: Statistical learning has been proposed as a powerful general learning mechanism that might be particularly useful in language acquisition.
source: Statistical learning has been proposed as a powerful general learning mechanism that might be particularly useful in language acquisition in order to extract words from the speech stream (Saffran et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Saffran et al., 1996.

claim: The exact model explaining statistical learning remains under-specified.
source: However, the exact model explaining statistical learning remains under-speciﬁed: What is computed remains unclear (Fló et al., 2022; Henin et al., 2021) and authors often tailored the computation to suit the paradigm (TPs in some studies, non-adjacent or backward TPs in others, biased transitions probabilities in network studies, etc.).
evidence: This is a claim about the state of the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The FEMM is a more general model that can account for results traditionally explained by the computation of local transitional probabilities and those that require the computation of long-distance dependencies.
source: We argue that the FEMM is a more general model that, beyond explaining community separation, as shown above, can also account for results traditionally explained by the computation of local transitional probabilities and those that require the computation of long-distance dependencies.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim proposed by the authors.

claim: The predictions of the FEMM are the same as those of the TP model in many tasks, notably in classical speech segmentation experiments.
source: Thus, the predictions of the FEMM are the same as those of the TP model in many tasks, notably in classical speech segmentation experiments, where a drop in TP signals word edges (Saffran et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the FEMM model, supported by citation.

claim: A bias estimation of transition probabilities following the FEMM is sensitive to non-adjacent dependencies and can explain the emergence of AxC structures.
source: However, a bias estimation of TPs following the FEMM is sensitive to non-adjacent dependencies and can explain the emergence of AxC structures.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the FEMM model.

claim: The FEMM can explain subjects' behavior in different kinds of network learning.
source: Additionally, as previous papers and our results show, the FEMM can also explain subjects' behavior in different kinds of network learning (Karuza et al., 2016; Lynn et al., 2020; Schapiro et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and the current study's results.

claim: Lynn et al., 2020, interpret the FEMM as errors in the associations between elements, whose probability decays with the distance between associated elements.
source: Lynn et al., 2020, interpret the FEMM as errors in the associations between elements, whose probability decays with the distance between associated elements.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lynn et al., 2020.

claim: Implementing the transition probabilities computation through Hebbian learning with a firing decay results in a comparable computation to the free energy model.
source: We proposed that implementing the TPs computation through Hebbian learning with a ﬁring decay results in a comparable computation to the free energy model.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal by the authors.

claim: A similar Hebbian learning approach enables to explain the sensitivity to backward transition probabilities reported in the literature.
source: Finally, a similar Hebbian learning approach enables to explain the sensitivity to backward TP reported in the literature (Endress and Johnson, 2021; Pelucchi et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Endress and Johnson, 2021; Pelucchi et al., 2009.

claim: The FEMM and its putative neural implementation through Hebbian rules unifies different proposals concerning statistical learning and network learning results under a common principle.
source: Thus, the FEMM and its putative neural implementation through Hebbian rules uniﬁes different proposals concerning statistical learning on the one hand and network learning results on the other hand, under a common principle.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim summarizing the contribution of the study.

claim: Many real-world networks have transitivity properties.
source: Unlike random networks, many real-world networks have transitivity properties (Girvan and Newman, 2002; Newman, 2006; Newman, 2003) - if A is connected to B and B to C, there is a high chance for A and C to be connected (a friend of my friend is likely to be my friend).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Girvan and Newman, 2002; Newman, 2006; Newman, 2003.

claim: Overgeneralizing enables faster learning.
source: Overgeneralizing enables faster learning. Overgeneralizing means accepting transitions congruent with the structure even before they appear in the stream. Thus, for short exposures, the estimation of the FEMM is closer to the real TP matrix than the estimation of the TP model based on the input because it infers transitions that have not been presented yet.
evidence: This is a theoretical argument about the advantages of the FEMM.

claim: Fast learning might be of importance for language acquisition, given that human infants are exposed to a limited amount of speech.
source: This fast learning might be of importance, for example, for language acquisition, given that human infants are exposed to a limited amount of speech.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the implications of the findings.

claim: The learning bias in extracting statistical information might subsequently be used to form abstract condensed network representations.
source: Adding to why humans have biased statistical learning, we propose that this learning bias in extracting statistical information might subsequently be used to form abstract condensed network representations.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The extraction of high-order structures might enable information compression in long-term memory.
source: In fact, the extraction of high-order structures might enable information compression in long-term memory.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Compressing information is a major advantage because of the computational cost and the pressure on memory to encode long sequences.
source: Because of the computational cost and the pressure on memory to encode long sequences, compressing information is a major advantage.
evidence: This is a theoretical argument based on general principles of cognition.

claim: Recent data showed that in some circumstances, humans' performances were highly sensitive to input compressibility.
source: Recent data (Al Roumi et al., 2021; Dehaene et al., 2014; Planton et al., 2021; Sablé-Meyer et al., 2022; Sablé-Meyer et al., 2021) showed that in some circumstances, humans' performances were highly sensitive to input compressibility, arguing for a condensed encoding of inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Al Roumi et al., 2021; Dehaene et al., 2014; Planton et al., 2021; Sablé-Meyer et al., 2022; Sablé-Meyer et al., 2021.

claim: A recent study using a graph perspective proposes that the representation of the abstract relational structure of a sequence and the mapping between node and stimuli identity could be factorized.
